cells.tense: You are in the work now, with your hands on what you are making.
cells.ask: Pause once mid-build and say what this thing will hold when it is done.
cells.core:
You're building something solid, and you're in it — hands on it, taking the weight, making it hold. Not forcing it past what it can carry. Your strength hasn't hardened yet; it's still the kind that knows its own cost, and the work comes back to you as yours.

Here, before anything has separated out, that solidity matters more than direction. One thing you're making well is feeding something the work won't hold on its own: the ability to stay near people while you build. You don't lose the build by pausing. Pause mid-build, say what this carries when it's finished, and see whether saying it changes the next step.
cells.sheetLine: You build what holds, and, holding, it holds you back.
cells.verb: building that holds by governed step, taking the weight only what is made to last
cells.place: the seed ground where nothing has separated out yet and every direction is still open

cells.tense: You will finish it before it has been started, and you are already bracing for the load.
cells.ask: Leave one thing unbuilt today and let someone else name the next move.
cells.core:
You're already building what isn't there yet. The next stage gets planned, fortified, made ready before the seed has even opened — and the load you're carrying is weight that hasn't arrived. That's the building bending forward, taking the future as if it were a wall you can get ahead of.

Bracing that hard isn't strength; it's strength reaching past what anything has asked of it. You can't will your way back by building harder or faster. Leave one thing unbuilt today, hand the next move to someone else, and let plain fairness decide: what's actually yours to carry, and what you picked up early so it couldn't surprise you. That keeps the build, and drops the brace.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying the future, and the future isn't here.

cells.tense: You stopped at a door that is already behind you, and you have not moved.
cells.ask: Finish one small thing today and stop at the finish, without starting the next.
cells.core:
There's something you started and didn't finish, and you're still in front of it — or in front of where it was. The building impulse didn't fail. The handoff did. You know what completion feels like, and some part of you won't move until whatever was left unfinished gets its end.

What's gone empty here isn't the want, it's the strength to hold. Don't push yourself into building something new — that just digs the same doorway. Finish one small thing today, stop at the finish, and let the release have its own place. Completing something, even a little, is what puts the strength back in the room.
cells.sheetLine: The door is behind you. You haven't moved.

cells.tense: You are already holding the room steady, and you call it just how things are.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, which part of the steady thing is yours.
cells.core:
You're keeping something standing — a household, a project, a rhythm other people lean on — and you don't count it as anything you did. It gets talked about like it runs itself, like it just keeps going. But the steady thing is still steady because you're holding it.

Strength that hasn't claimed itself isn't weak; it's unmarked. The work is real and it's yours, and nobody has said so, including you. Say it once, plainly, which part is yours — not pride, just saying what is true. The radiance comes after that, from something that's actually finished and actually kept, and it doesn't need the whole room to agree.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding it steady and calling it nothing you did.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my first draft was that the person is aware of and choosing among the possibilities in the seat; the record says the seat is possibility before differentiation, so awareness of the choosing is not given, and a reader could reasonably say 'I don't feel like I'm sorting options, I just keep building.' The ask survives being wrong because it is an act of pause and holds whatever the true state is, and the sentence that serves me more than them was any line about 'knowing what you're building toward' — cut, since it flatters the seat rather than describing it.
